taxonomyNote: Tennessee WRA spells the epithet 'sexlineata' and SREL uses Cnemidophorus [Aspidoscelis]; NatureServe uses Aspidoscelis sexlineatus (older literature places racerunners in Cnemidophorus).
fieldMarks: Long, slender, fast lizard 6-9.5 in with six light stripes (yellow, white, grey or pale blue) running from head onto the tail on a dark brown, black or dark grey ground colour.
Tail is grey or brown, rougher in feel and often shows only one or two light stripes on its side; skinks, which look similar, have smooth shiny scales.
Belly is white to salmon-pink in females and bluish in males; males become bluer in the breeding season and have a broader head, females a heavier body.
Hatchlings resemble adults but have pale blue tails and distinct yellow stripes.
behavior: Active only in warm daylight and seeks shelter during the hottest midday period in summer; often active at body temperatures near 100 F.
Emerges later from winter burrows than many lizards; activity runs May-September in the north and longer in the south.
Eats insects, spiders and snails; shelters underground or under rocks and other objects, and sometimes escapes by submerging in water.
Eggs are laid in nests dug in soft soil or sawdust or under logs, 1-3 clutches of 1-6 eggs May-August.
habitat: Open, dry, sunny habitats with loose sandy or gravelly soil and sparse vegetation: grassland, sandhills, stream floodplains, rocky slopes at mountain bases, woodland edges, dunes, glades, rock quarries and roadsides.
range: NatureServe lists it across the central and southeastern US, from Maryland, Michigan, Wisconsin and Wyoming south to Florida, Texas and New Mexico; it is not recorded for Canada.
